## Discussion {#discussion}

Our silicon sampling forecast puts the median number of Democratic governors at `{python} h["dem_median"]`, with a `{python} h["p_dem_majority"]` chance that Democrats hold 26 or more seats and a `{python} h["p_rep_majority"]` chance for Republicans.  Concerning the overall result, our forecast aligns with that of the professional forecasters. Assuming that the outcome of each race would be in favor of whichever candidate the forecasters favor in their October ratings, as assembled on Wikipedia [@wikipediapolls], the ratings of Cook Political Report would result in 24 to 28 governors for Democrats, and those of Sabato's Crystal Ball and Silver Bulletin – 26 to 28. Nevertheless, there are two states where we forecast differently from professional forecasters. This section attempts to answer the question whether such a difference indicates that we discovered something the experts overlooked or that we overstepped the boundaries of our approach.

### The total agrees with the experts, two races do not

In every race where the majority of the seven rating agencies in our dataset favor one party, we favor that party, except for two races. Georgia (even odds), Nevada (Republican 53%), and Ohio (Democrat 59%) are toss-ups in our assessment and also rated so by the agencies. In these two cases, however, we see different preferences from the agencies.

In Alaska we give the Republican candidate 67% chance. There are five out of seven agencies who rate this race as favoring Democrats while Silver Bulletin rates this race as Solidly Democratic. At least some part of the difference is due to the way we model the race. Alaska uses ranked choice voting and we treat the final round of voting by adding up the percentage share of three Republican candidates. This implies that all Republicans voted rank another Republican as the second choice while none of Republicans voted for the Democrat candidate. The polls, when summed in the same way, show an advantage of Republicans by 1.4 points.

The probability that the Democrat beats the incumbent, Phil Scott, is 62% in Vermont. All seven agencies predict a win for Phil Scott. The polls predict a lead for him by 2.5 points, while the corrected AI surveys predict a lead for the Democrat by 8.5. Vermont is one of the most Democratic states in America. If we have a persona that leans Democratic, he will vote for the Democrat no matter what the record of the Republican running is. The personas do not capture Scott's appeal to Democrats, and the reason is shown below.

In case the two elections took place according to the agencies' predictions, Democrats would take Alaska and lose Vermont. There are 21 races in which we favor Democrats. Adding the 6 governors not running in their own states, we have 27. The two discrepancies offset each other. A forecast can agree with the experts on the top line while disagreeing with them on individual races, making the seats tally an unreliable measure of a technique's validity.

### The synthetic voters know party, not candidates

Argyle et al. [-@argyle2023] found that GPT-3, given the background of real survey respondents, reproduced how groups of Americans voted. They called this "algorithmic fidelity". Our results support the coarse version of that claim. Across the 33 states with polls, the raw AI-survey margin correlates 0.85 with the poll average (@fig-silicon-polls), so the models rank the states much as the polls do.

The finer version fails to apply. When we regress the poll margin on the AI-survey margin, the slope is 0.58: the AI surveys spread the states too far apart. In the AI surveys, Massachusetts is D+38 and D+25 in the polls; Idaho is R+50 against R+22. Between 96.5% and 98.4% of the Democratic and Republican validation personas vote for their own party's candidate, depending on the model. Removing party from the persona changes 16% to 20% of the votes, while removing any reference to incumbency affects 3% to 6%, about the same as asking the identical question twice (4% to 5%). The models choose a candidate by party affiliation and do not care about incumbency at all. Bisbee et al. [-@bisbee2024] showed the same phenomenon to occur with ChatGPT: while its synthetic answers corresponded to the average opinion, there was not enough variance. Wang et al. [-@wang2025] call this phenomenon flattening, where the model treats all members of a group as its archetype. A state full of typical partisans is a safer state than a real one, which is what our slope shows.

Moreover, these misses go against the narrative of bias. Santurkar et al. [-@santurkar2023] noted that fine-tuned language models are more likely to be biased towards liberals with high education levels in America. While our surveys lean toward Republicans on average by 7.2 percentage points than polls do, in New Hampshire our surveys show an advantage of 4.8 points to the Democrat while polls favor incumbent Republican Kelly Ayotte by 10.6 percentage points, and in Vermont, our surveys are again tilted towards the Democrat.  Pennsylvania misses the other way: D+3.6 in the AI survey against D+27 in the polls for the Democratic incumbent, Josh Shapiro. One lean cannot explain such three misses. But ignoring the incumbency effect can – in each state, our surveys are close to where just considering the party predicts while polls have a governor taking voters from the other party.
